papers.title: Efforts to Increase Community Participation in Agroforestry Land Conservation on the Slopes of Mount Muria
papers.source: Journal of Business Social and Technology
papers.summary: Background: The slopes of Mount Muria serve as a water catchment area, a habitat for biodiversity, and a source of community livelihoods through agroforestry. However, land-use conversion, non-conservation-oriented cultivation practices, erosion, and landslides threaten the sustainability of these areas. Objective: This study aims to describe community activities on agroforestry land, identify the forms and assess the levels of community participation, and formulate strategies to strengthen participation in agroforestry land conservation in Colo Village, Dawe Subdistrict, Kudus Regency. Methods: A descriptive quantitative approach with a cross-sectional survey design was employed. From a population of 454 coffee farmers, 46 respondents were selected through proportional random sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires, observations, interviews, and documentation and were analyzed using descriptive percentages based on Abu Huraerah’s forms of participation and Arnstein’s Ladder of Citizen Participation. Results: Community participation was classified as good, with a score of 78.57%. Material contributions (85.76%) and labor contributions (81.30%) were dominant, while skills contributions (74.13%) required further strengthening. The level of participation was also categorized as good, with an overall score of 70.96%, comprising Nonparticipation (77.81%), Citizen Power (71.06%), and Tokenism (66.30%). Among the indicators, Information received the lowest score (60.51%). These findings demonstrate that conservation outcomes depend on the quality of community involvement throughout the land-management process. Conclusion: The study supports a community-empowerment-based conservation education approach and recommends strengthening farmer-group institutions, participatory extension services, technical skills, and information transparency to improve community participation in agroforestry land conservation.

papers.title: The use of near-surface geophysics for monitoring slopes that affect transport infrastructure
papers.summary: Landslides on transportation networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in response to environmental change, at the same time as demand placed on road and rail infrastructure is growing in line with population growth and economic development. To minimise the impact of slope instability on vital transport infrastructure, as well as on terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, public safety, communities, local heritage, and the economy, and to better inform decision making, there is a need for remote-condition-monitoring systems to reveal processes that are precursors to slope failure. Here, the application of a novel electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) system (Proactive infrastructure Monitoring and Evaluation (PRIME)) for monitoring unstable slopes that affect transport infrastructure is examined. The system provides near-real-time data collection via a telemetric link. 4-Dimensional resistivity models (3-D with a time-lapse element) are presented in the context of moisture content and soil suction, two parameters known to influence slope stability. Building upon relationships evident in the field, the development of laboratory-based petrophysical relationships that relate electrical resistivity to moisture content and soil suction directly is also discussed. 4-D ERT models were calibrated using these petrophysical relationships to provide insights into complex spatial and temporal variations in moisture content and soil suction. Two study areas are considered here, enabling different controls on electrical resistivity to be examined. The Ripley Landslide in the Thompson River Valley, British Columbia, Canada, threatens the serviceability of two national railway lines. Here, 4-D ERT models reveal complex hydrogeological pathways, providing new insights into the subsurface processes in an active, natural landslide. papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Main Info A variety of cryogenic slope processes, including ALDS (active-layer detachment slides) and RTS (retrogressive thaw slumps), occur in the north of West Siberia. Previous research into these processes only partly cover the Yenisei North, and only in the context of identifying the RTS, but not ALDS. This region covers more than 60,000 km2, where we mapped ALDS and RTS locations using remote sensing imagery from 2000 to 2025. We identified the spatial patterns and determining factors that control the distribution of both types of cryogenic landslide along a latitudinal regiongradient spanning approximately 450 km from the Arctic tundra to the southern forest tundra. papers.title: Synergising local geo-environmental characteristics with spatial context for enhancing landslide susceptibility mapping
papers.summary: Data-driven methods are widely used in landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) because they can effectively model the complex relationships between landslides and geo-environmental conditions. Existing data-driven approaches generally follow two types of data representations. Pixel-based models focus solely on the geo-environmental characteristics of a specific landslide but neglect the influence of its surrounding environment. Patch-based models incorporate surrounding spatial context but may include pixels with weak or no spatial relevance to the target landslide location. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion (LGSCF) strategy, which synergises the geo-environmental characteristics of landslide points with their corresponding spatial context through a feature-wise modulation mechanism. We tested the LGSCF strategy by integrating it into several representative convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, creating nine different LGSCF-based models. The primary study area covers approximately 2644 km² across Jenai and Sinyi Townships in Nantou County, Taiwan, and the dataset comprises 5332 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples. The results show that LGSCF-based models consistently outperform their corresponding baselines, achieving F1-scores up to 87.09% and AUC values up to 0.9472. Furthermore, the susceptibility maps produced by LGSCF-based models show that known landslides are more accurately concentrated in “very high” susceptibility zones with fewer misclassifications. These findings demonstrate that our fusion strategy can significantly improve the accuracy of landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.summary: BigLeak Archaeology BigLeak Archaeology V1.3 – A Formally Falsifiable Compression Protocol for Symbolic Systems This independent research document tests the hypothesis of a domain-general cognitive compression protocol underlying prehistoric symbolic clusters. We define a 5-slot essence E = {σ Origin, κ Relation, π Individuation, τ Time, γ Transition} and operationalize compliance through four explicit axioms: |E|=5, E⊂V, |V|≥13 (implements |V|/|E|≥2.5), and S(E)/S(V) ∈ [0.6;0.7]. Entropy calculations, codebook V1-V4 and a runnable Python evaluator are included for full reproducibility (Cohen K_IRR = 0.72). N=15 symbolic clusters from 18,000 BP to 1000 AD across four continents pass all axioms; a contrast sample of 4 complex structures passes 0/4, demonstrating discriminant validity. Primary is now the landslide-resilient Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum, Malta (FS≈183.6, <1% noise, carved from in situ limestone bedrock), with Chauvet Cave and Yazılıkaya as secondary / tertiary. papers.title: Initiation thresholds and statistical properties of rainfall-induced landslides under centennial-scale variations in land use and land cover and rainfall characteristics
AI-based procedure for extracting spatial and temporal information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources
papers.summary: Abstract Comprehensive landslide catalogues require accurate and reproducible spatial and temporal information, yet manual extraction from textual sources is time-consuming and affected by inter- and intra-operator variability. We present AIDE4LAND (Artificial Intelligence-based procedure for Data Extraction for LANDslides), a novel structured procedure that combines Large Language Models and prompt engineering to automatically extract temporal and spatial information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources. The procedure is organized as a two-step process: (i) temporal extraction, which reconstructs the date and time of occurrence according to explicit hierarchical rules and assigns standardized temporal accuracy levels, and (ii) spatial extraction, which progressively determines geographic coordinates through structured queries and reverse-geocoding validation using OpenStreetMap APIs via Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol. The workflow was developed through iterative prompt-refinement cycles, involving 2162 tests conducted on 725 textual sources (664 written in Italian and 61 in English) published between 2011 and 2025. Validation of AIDE4LAND outputs against a manually compiled expert dataset revealed a high level of agreement, with 87% of cases demonstrating maximum concordance in terms of temporal and spatial attribution. By combining standardized rules, explicit accuracy classification, and automated consistency checks, AIDE4LAND formalizes expert reasoning into transparent and reproducible procedural rules, thereby reducing interpretative variability and ensuring transparent and systematic traceability in the decision process. The procedure significantly accelerates catalogue updates and provides a transferable and reproducible methodological framework for constructing structured rainfall-induced landslide catalogues, supporting hazard assessment, rainfall-threshold definition, and early warning applications.

papers.title: Guangdong rainfall-induced landslide inventory and environmental variables for latent-regime analysis
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset contains the processed research data supporting the study “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The dataset comprises 2,025 rainfall-related landslide records from Guangdong Province, South China, together with the environmental variables used to investigate delayed landslide responses to rainfall forcing. The dataset includes landslide identifiers and locations, occurrence and rainfall-event timing information, landslide lag time, soil thickness, slope, aspect, lithology, and antecedent cumulative rainfall over 3-h, 6-h, 12-h, 1-day, 2-day, and 3-day windows. Figure-level data and model-output files used to evaluate the analyses reported in the manuscript are also provided. The dataset supports the statistical analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, model selection, environmental attribution, and figure generation presented in the manuscript. A data dictionary describing the variables, units, and processing information is included in the archive. Original third-party source records subject to redistribution restrictions are not redistributed in this archive. Their provenance and access conditions are documented in the accompanying documentation.

papers.title: Forensic back-analysis of a reactivated deep-seated landslide in volcanic residual soils of the Cisumdawu highway KM 178, Indonesia
papers.summary: Abstract Background This study is a forensic back-analysis of the 2021 embankment failure at KM 178 of the Cisumdawu Highway, Indonesia. The post-failure investigation identified weak subsurface materials but no discrete failure horizon, and the mechanism was never established. Six independent lines of field evidence were assembled, from UAV LiDAR geomorphology to paired triaxial and direct shear testing. A two-dimensional Morgenstern–Price model was built with the failure surface fixed from that evidence while material parameters were calibrated. Pore pressure was represented as a material-specific ratio rather than a piezometric surface, the residual soil permeability being too low to transmit storm rainfall to depth. Uncertainty was propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. Results The alignment crosses a valley floored by relict landslide deposits, with arcuate paleo-scarps on the upper slope. The weathering profile grades from residual silty clay through residual silty sand to weathered tuff, placing a granular horizon within low-permeability clay, so permeability is not monotonic with depth. Inclinometers installed after the rupture intercepted a shear horizon at 559 and 536 m elevation, recording 15 cm and 10 cm of cumulative wet-season displacement, while the instrument monitored during the dry season recorded none. Deeper horizons remain active but could not be traced laterally, indicating a larger relict complex. That horizon coincides with N-SPT below 10 enclosed within material returning 20 to 30, a strength inversion weathering cannot produce, and with gravelly deposits of low resistivity. Without imposed pore pressure it is not the critical surface, returning 1.40 against 1.29 for a shallower surface within the embankment. It becomes critical only when the pore-pressure ratio reaches about 0.37, at an operational friction angle of 20.5°, below the measured peak of 29°. papers.title: Peer Review Report For: Physical and Mechanical Characteristics of Soil as a Controlling Factor in Landslides in Curug Panjang Village, Cihuni Hamlet, Lebak, Banten: Analysis of Distribution, Normality, and Inter-parameter Relationships [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
papers.summary: Background Landslide occurrence is strongly influenced by the physical and mechanical properties of subsurface soil; this study evaluates these properties in residual soil from Kampung Cihuni, Lebak Regency, as a controlling factor in landslides. Methods Thirty residual soil samples were collected at a depth of 0–1 m using a grid sampling method. Laboratory testing covered natural water content (w); specific gravity and unit weight, used to derive void ratio (e); the plasticity index (PI) from the Atterberg limits; and Unconsolidated Undrained (UU) triaxial testing for cohesion (c) and internal friction angle (φ). The distribution of each parameter was evaluated using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, while inter-parameter relationships were analysed using linear regression (R 2 ) and Spearman correlation (ρ). Results The Shapiro-Wilk test showed that cohesion (c) and void ratio (e) are normally distributed, whereas water content (w), PI, and friction angle (φ) are not. PI values for the plastic samples (n = 26) ranged from 13.8% to 86.7%, and φ ranged from 5.48° to 20.5°; the relationship between the two was weakly positive (R 2 = 0.151, p = 0.050; Spearman ρ = 0.244, p = 0.229). Cohesion ranged from 4.41–52.47 kPa but showed a very weak, non-significant relationship with water content (R 2 = 0.028, p = 0.376), as did void ratio with φ (R 2 = 0.089, p = 0.110). Conclusions Relationships among the physical and mechanical parameters were weak and mostly non-significant, so the reduction in soil shear strength cannot be explained by any single parameter alone. Because the UU triaxial test represents total-stress conditions, it cannot directly explain rainfall infiltration and pore-water pressure change as a landslide trigger, though it offers an initial picture of the residual soil’s engineering characteristics as a controlling factor in the area’s landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: Permafrost Monitoring in the Central Alaska Network of National Parks
papers.summary: The three national park units which comprise the National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring Program’s Central Alaska Network (CAKN: Wrangell-St. Elias, Denali, and Yukon-Charley Rivers) are underlain by permafrost—ground that remains at or below 0°C for at least two, but typically many, years. Much of that permafrost, however, is geographically discontinuous, thin, and close to the melting point of water. Under the warming conditions that characterize these parks, permafrost thaw is likely to have significant impacts on the landscapes of these parks. These impacts may include development of thermokarst, landslides and slumping, changes in hydrology and vegetation, growth and/or drainage of lakes, enhanced release of greenhouse gases, and decay of characteristic permafrost features like pingos and rock glaciers. The CAKN permafrost monitoring program is designed to monitor a subset of these changes over multiple decades, and focuses on tracking changes in the thermal and physical state of permafrost. Collected data will contribute directly to the Global Terrestrial Network for Permafrost, the primary international permafrost monitoring program. Thermal changes will be monitored with a broad network of shallow (<3 m) soil temperature measurements, and also with temperature measurements from a single deep (29-70 m) borehole adjacent to each park. These measurements will mostly be conducted in collaboration with existing monitoring programs to leverage existing resources. Physical changes will be monitored with a network of active layer thickness measurements that use late-summer mechanical probing to determine maximum thaw depth on fine-grained permafrost soils. The thaw depth measurements will be co-located with survey-grade differential global positioning system (dGPS) surveys of soil surface elevation to detect thaw-related subsidence. papers.title: Integrating Kernel-Based Machine Learning Techniques with Geospatial Analysis for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Sikkim, India
papers.source: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Spatial machine learning modelling reveals that soil indicators and tree type best explain shallow landslide release
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: The exploration of shallow landslide susceptibility is often impaired by biased landslide inventories, and by over-optimistic performance metrics linked to inadequate models. Here, we use a systematically mapped event inventory of 571 shallow landslides triggered in southern Norway and apply 32 gradient boosted decision tree models to rigorously test the effects of (1) a nested vs. simple cross-validation strategy, (2) spatial vs. non-spatial models, (3) four different cross-validation sampling strategies which were applied on (4) full vs. forest-only datasets. Model evaluation shows that models with random cross-validation provided the highest test performance metrics but did not account for autocorrelation and were likely over-optimistic. The spatial models with spatial cross-validation reduced autocorrelation in the model residuals at the expense of predictive power. Although no model emerged as optimal, findings across models suggest that important explanatory factors like elevation, aspect and bedrock weatherability serve as soil indicators, illustrating a need for improved datasets for soil thickness and heterogeneity. In the forest-only models, tree type was consistently an important predictor, with higher landslide susceptibility in deciduous forest, illustrating the potential of forest variables and forest-specific threshold values in shallow landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: Silent forces rising risks: A systematic review of natural hazards, cascading processes and emerging risk in the Himalaya
papers.source: International Journal of Geography Geology and Environment
papers.summary: Background: The Himalaya is the youngest, highest and most tectonically and climatically active mountain belt on Earth. Hazard prone environments create by large human populations. Traditionally, earthquakes, rainfall- and earthquake triggered landslides, debris flows, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF), permafrost degradation, rock ice avalanches and snow avalanches have been studied as separate hazard classes. Yet field evidence from recent disasters shows that these events are frequently linked in cascading and compounding sequences. Objective: This review synthesizes peer-reviewed and institutional literature on natural hazards and emerging cascading risk across the Himalayan arc with emphasis on (i) the geological and climatic drivers of individual hazard types (ii) documented cascading and compound hazard pathways, (iii) the growing exposure of settlements and infrastructure and (iv) research and risk management gaps. Methods: A structured systematic literature review was undertaken. Academic search platforms (Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, Nature Portfolio journals, Copernicus/NHESS, MDPI, AGU/Wiley, Frontiers) and institutional repositories (ICIMOD/HKH library, USGS, World Bank, UNDP) were searched using combinations of terms relating to Himalayan hazards, cascading and compound risk, glacial lake outburst floods, seismicity, permafrost and disaster risk reduction for literature published mainly between 2000 and 2026. Because this review draws on open-web-indexed academic search rather than paid bibliographic databases. It is presented as a structured systematic analysis; the eligibility screening, source list and limitations of this approach are stated explicitly in the Methods section. papers.title: Python and Stan code for Bayesian latent-regime analysis of delayed rainfall-induced landslides
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This software archive contains the Python and Stan source code used for the analyses reported in the Earth's Future manuscript “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The software implements data preprocessing, environmental-control analyses, principal component analysis, soil-thickness and lag-time analyses, predictor–lag relationships, correlation and Mantel analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, WAIC-based model selection, posterior predictive checks, regime–soil-thickness analyses, Random Forest and XGBoost environmental attribution, SHAP analysis, and generation of the main and supplementary figures. The Bayesian latent-regime analysis is implemented using Stan and CmdStanPy. Candidate numbers of latent regimes are evaluated using WAIC, with the selected model subsequently used for posterior regime inference and environmental attribution. Version 1.0.0 corresponds to the software release associated with the manuscript submitted to Earth's Future. papers.title: Empirically informed AHP-FR modeling for multi-hazard susceptibility mapping in a mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Abstract Mountainous transport corridors are increasingly exposed to interacting natural hazards that intensify infrastructure, socio-economic, and land-use risks. However, most susceptibility assessments for high-mountain corridors still focus on single hazards or rely heavily on expert-based weighting, which can introduce subjectivity into spatial decision-making. This study develops an empirically informed Analytical Hierarchy Process–Frequency Ratio (AHP-FR) framework for integrated landslide, debris-flow, and flood susceptibility mapping along the Barakhan–Gilgit–Juglot section of the northern China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The main methodological contribution is the use of frequency-ratio-derived empirical evidence that was integrated with AHP-derived factor weights to calculate final subclass weights and thereby reducing reliance on purely subjective expert judgment. Field surveys, remote sensing datasets, historical hazard inventories, and 12 conditioning factors were integrated in a GIS environment to generate single-hazard susceptibility maps and an eight-class multi-hazard susceptibility map. Independent ROC-AUC validation showed acceptable to very good predictive performance, with AUC values of 0.803 for landslides, 0.762 for debris flows, and 0.872 for floods. The results indicate that 63% of the corridor is exposed to one or more hazards, including 59% exposed to two or more overlapping hazards; 41% are co-susceptible to landslides and debris flows, while 37% falls within the no/very low multi-hazard susceptibility class. The spatial outputs identify major hazard-prone sections, including Attabad, Chalt, and Passu, providing practical guidance for road-maintenance prioritization, slope-stabilization planning, drainage improvement, and emergency preparedness. The added value of this study lies in combining empirical FR-based weighting with AHP and translating separate hazard maps into explicit multi-hazard combination classes, offering a repro

papers.title: Effects of mapping units on landslide susceptibility assessment: a comparative analysis of slope units and raster cells
papers.summary: The choice of spatial mapping units substantially shapes the accuracy, spatial detail, and interpretability of landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA). To investigate how mapping-unit selection affects LSA performance, this study used Hejing County, Xinjiang, China, as a case study. Based on a historical landslide inventory and a multi-source environmental-factor database, two mapping-unit schemes were constructed: 30 m raster cells and slope units extracted through a hydrology-based delineation method. Based on twelve selected conditioning factors, landslide susceptibility was modeled using four machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), and XGBoost. In addition, the SHAP method was applied to examine differences in model decision mechanisms and factor contributions between the two mapping-unit schemes. The findings indicate that both mapping-unit schemes are capable of representing the spatial variability of LSA across the study area. The raster-cell-based scheme generally showed better predictive performance, with the mean AUC of the four models increasing from 0.798 under the slope-unit scheme to 0.859 under the raster-cell scheme. This indicates that raster cells are more effective in capturing localized environmental heterogeneity and small-scale high-susceptibility patches. In contrast, the slope-unit-based scheme reduced inter-model performance differences and generated more spatially continuous and stable susceptibility zonation consistent with natural slope boundaries. SHAP analysis further indicates that the dominant conditioning factors were generally consistent between the two schemes; however, raster-cell-based models were more sensitive to localized disturbances and micro-topographic variability, whereas slope-unit-based models emphasized the integrated constraints of geomorphological structure and hydrological processes. papers.title: Dynamic response and damage mechanism of deep overburden layer slope based on shaking table tests
papers.summary: The mountain areas of southwest China are widely covered with loose fractured rock bodies, which are prone to large-scale landslides under seismic action. It is known that the response of the acceleration amplification factor field is closely related to the seismic damage state of the overburden. In order to study the dynamic response and damage mechanism of overburden layer slopes under seismic action, a deep base-covered slope model containing two layers of stacks is used as a prototype in this study, and a series of shaking-table modeling experiments of progressive damage of earthquake-induced slopes are carried out. The cumulative seismic damage deformation process of the slope overburden was identified based on embedded sensors and Particle Image Velocimetry technology, and the energy transfer mechanism of the process was revealed by Hilbert Huang transform. The results show that the non-coherent motion (vibration frequency difference) between the shallow overburden layer-thick overburden layer-bedrock layer is the main controlling factor inducing the slope landslide, and the damage form of the deep overburden slope manifests itself in the form of the trailing edge sliding and extruding the central shear out. The damage starts from the back edge of the slope with increasing seismic intensity and gradually moves toward the middle to lower part of the slope, while extending from the surface to the deeper part of the slope.

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning-Based Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment and Upazila-Level Intervention Prioritization in the Chattogram Region, Bangladesh
papers.summary: The increasing occurrence of natural hazards, either individually or in combination, has intensified disaster risk worldwide, with the Chattogram Region of Bangladesh representing a prominent multi-hazard hotspot where earthquakes, landslides, and floods frequently coexist. An interpretable GIS–ML-based multi-hazard risk assessment (MHRA) framework was developed to generate earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility zones (EQSZ, LSSZ, and FSZ) using ensemble machine learning algorithms, with model predictions explained through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The resulting susceptibility maps were integrated into a Multi-Hazard Index, which was then combined with a Vulnerability Index to produce the final Multi-Hazard Risk Zone (MHRZ). GBM achieved the highest predictive performance for earthquake (AUC = 0.799) and landslide (AUC = 0.786), whereas RF performed best for flood susceptibility (AUC = 0.917). SHAP identified shear-wave velocity (Vs30), Soil Moisture Index, and elevation as the most influential predictors of earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility, respectively. Although the eastern hill districts exhibited the highest multi-hazard susceptibility, the MHRZ identified the densely populated upazilas of Chattogram and Cox's Bazar as the highest-risk areas because socio-economic vulnerability outweighed comparatively moderate hazard susceptibility. Approximately 55.10% of the study area fell within the very low to low-risk classes, whereas only 21.49% fell within the high-to-very-high-risk classes, highlighting the critical role of socio-economic vulnerability in shaping regional disaster risk. The proposed MHRA framework offers a methodologically transferable basis for evidence-based disaster risk reduction (DRR) by enabling upazila-level policy screening, preliminary DRR intervention prioritization, and resilient spatial planning in multi-hazard, data-scarce regions.

papers.title: Analyzing Seismic and Acoustic Signals with Network-Based Coherence and Phase
papers.summary: Abstract The seismoacoustic wavefield contains a variety of signals that can be challenging to detect and characterize, particularly those that are weak, emergent, or visible only on a subset of stations. A few examples of such sources include volcanic and tectonic tremor, anthropogenic noise, landslides, and glaciers. Here, we present network-based coherence—a simple cross-spectral method applicable to both seismic and acoustic sensors in network or array configurations. The method enhances signals that are coherent across multiple stations while suppressing noise unique to individual sensors, enabling robust detection of subtle seismoacoustic sources. Building on this, we introduce a phase-based acoustic source localization method that uses interstation phase differences to locate non-impulsive signals. We demonstrate these methods on data from an operational volcano seismic network and an International Monitoring System infrasound array. At Mount Spurr, Alaska, seismic network coherence reveals weak, ephemeral tremor during a period of unrest in 2024–2025. At the infrasound array I53US, array coherence identifies monochromatic and frequency-gliding noise sources, and phase-based location attributes a persistent ∼2 Hz signal to a nearby power plant. We envision this approach as a tool for data quality control, volcano monitoring, and noise assessment across seismic or acoustic networks and arrays.

papers.title: Climate Change and Environmental Degradation: The 2023 Earthquake in Turkey and Syria
papers.summary: This chapter provides an in-depth analysis of the 2023 earthquake that struck Turkey and Syria, focusing on its seismological, humanitarian, socioeconomic, public health, and environmental impacts. It begins with an overview of the geographic and geological factors that underpin the region&s;s vulnerability to seismic activity. The chapter explores the earthquake&s;s magnitude, depth, tectonic features, aftershock activity, and comparisons with past seismic events in the region. A subsequent section discusses rapid response efforts by local and international organizations, the challenges faced by rescue teams, and the provision of medical and psychological support for survivors. The socioeconomic repercussions are analyzed, with emphasis on impacts on local economies, housing, and long-term developmental challenges posed by displacement. The chapter also addresses significant public health concerns, such as sanitation and mental health issues, that emerged in the aftermath. Finally, it examines the environmental toll, including changes to natural landscapes, landslides, soil liquefaction, and potential long-term ecological consequences. This concise chapter aims to offer insights into the complex interplay between natural disasters and human resilience in the face of catastrophic events.

papers.title: Automated Landslide Scar Detection in the Himalayan Region Using Satellite Imagery and YOLO-Based Deep Learning Models
papers.source: Journal of the Geological Society of India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Landslides in the Himalayan region are the most serious hazards due to their destructive consequences in the context of life and the economy. More landslides are anticipated based on the present environmental and climatic scenario. Hence, a landslide information detection model is the foremost for hazard risk assessment. The application of deep learning algorithms in hazard analysis has gained significant attention worldwide. Moreover, remote sensing technology has emerged as a critical tool in diverse applications. Therefore, this study leverages the recent scientific and technological developments for extracting landslide-related information. We applied four YOLO (You Only Look Once) models, specifically YOLOv5, YOLOv6, YOLOv7, and YOLOv8, alongside eleven additional YOLO variants to detect landslide scars from satellite imagery. The study focuses on the Greater Himalayan Range, Nepal, utilising a dataset of 275 satellite images, divided into training, validation, and testing sets. The standard quantitative indicators, i.e., precision, recall, F-score, and mean average precision (mAP), are used for evaluation. The results indicate that YOLOv8 achieved the highest accuracy (F-score: 0.857), followed by YOLOv5, YOLOv7, and YOLOv6. These findings highlight the potential of YOLO-based models for rapid and accurate landslide detection, contributing to efficient hazard assessment and disaster response efforts.

papers.title: Voter Switching and Policy Preferences: Evidence from Japan's 2025–2026 Elections
papers.source: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
papers.summary: This study examines vote switching between Japan’s July 2025 House of Councilors and February 2026 House of Representatives elections. The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) suffered a major defeat in 2025 and then achieved a landslide victory in 2026 under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who adopted a moderate but firmly immigration-restrictive platform. Using a survey of 14,000 respondents and multinomial logit and probit models, we analyze party choice and vote switching. The major findings are as follows: (1) anti-consumption-tax attitudes are negatively associated with voting for the LDP and positively associated with voting for the right-wing Sanseito Party; (2) less opposition to foreigners as workplace colleagues relative to neighbors is positively associated with the probability of voting for the right-wing Sanseito Party; and (3) among voters for the right-wing Sanseito Party in 2025, less opposition to foreigners is positively associated with switching to the LDP in 2026.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of frequency ratio and index of entropy models for landslides susceptibility mapping of Dikhow river basin, Northeast India
papers.summary: Landslide Susceptible Mapping is a significant approach in hilly regions for delineating the potential areas for landslide occurrence. North-eastern states of India are most prone to landslides due to intense monsoonal rainfall, complex geology, and increasing anthropogenic activities. A significant portion of the Dikhow River Basin lies within the hilly regions of Nagaland, where intense monsoonal rainfall and fragile geological conditions trigger slope instability. Numerous reported landslide incidents highlight the severity of this disaster in this region. This research focuses on the comparative assessment of two landslide susceptibility maps generated from two bivariate models, namely (i) Frequency Ratio (FR) and (ii) Index of Entropy (IOE), in the Dikhow River Basin by integrating 12 landslide triggering factors and 632 landslide inventories using Geospatial Technology. The generated Landslide Susceptibility Map has been categorized into five hierarchical classes, from very low to very high, using the natural-break classification system. The study indicated that 19.9% and 8.4% of the study area correspond to very high susceptibility to landslides by FR and IOE, respectively. The validation results illustrated satisfactory performance for both models with AUC values of 0.81 and 0.79 for the training datasets, and 0.82 and 0.8 for the testing datasets, respectively. R-index values indicate that 64.81% (FR) and 60.25% (IOE) of landslide occurrences were associated with very high susceptibility classes. The validation process reveals that the FR has better success in comparison to the IOE model. In order to reduce the negative effects of landslide hazards, the suggested research will assist government, policymakers, and decision-makers in managing and mitigating the adverse consequences of landslides.

THE INFLUENCE OF THE POROSITY COEFFICIENT (RU) ON THE SAFETY FACTOR (Fs) WITH THE APPLICATION OF NUMERICAL METHODS.
papers.summary: A landslide can occur as a result of natural changes in the geological environment of a slope (changes in the groundwater regime, erosion, earthquake action), or as a result of human activities (removal of vegetation and positive root activity, filling and excavation in the process of road construction, additional loads placed on slopes due to the erection of buildings or road fillings, bridge construction, piles of waste material). When the mass of soil on a slope cannot ensure the balance of the forces acting on it, a landslide occurs, the area of the mass that is involved in the landslide is called a landslide body. When a slope landslide occurs, it is clear that there is a lack or weakening of the shear resistance of the sliding surface in order to maintain the equilibrium of the sliding body. The calculations of the safety factor are usually carried out according to the methods of limit equilibrium and the arcuate sliding surface. In the case of more complicated tasks (more complex, more complex conditions, the state of the rock mass and the size of the object) their solution by limit equilibrium methods is called into question. In such cases, numerical methods of calculation are also implemented, any of the methods for calculating the full state of stress and deformation of the given model. After that, the results obtained by the limit equilibrium methods are compared and the final conclusions are drawn by numerical methods.

papers.title: Uses of Artificial Intelligence In Geography
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in the field of Geography. It helps geographers collect, process, analyze, and interpret large amounts of geographical data quickly and accurately. AI is widely used with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Remote Sensing, satellite images, GPS, and spatial databases. It can help in land-use and land-cover mapping, urban planning, population analysis, disaster management, climate studies, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. AI-based techniques such as machine learning and deep learning can identify patterns and changes in geographical areas that may be difficult to detect through traditional methods. AI also helps in predicting natural hazards such as floods, droughts, landslides, and forest fires. In urban areas, it supports transportation planning, infrastructure development, and smart-city management. In agriculture, AI can assist in crop monitoring, soil analysis, and yield prediction. However, the effective use of AI requires reliable data, skilled users, proper technology, and attention to data privacy and accuracy. Thus, Artificial Intelligence has great potential to improve geographical research, spatial analysis, planning, and sustainable development.

papers.title: Reply on RC3
papers.summary: Abstract. Regional landslide susceptibility mapping generally treats landslide/non-landslide discrimination as a binary learning task and subsequently divides predicted probabilities into several qualitative classes. This two-stage strategy does not directly represent the susceptibility gradient and may therefore reduce the spatial concentration of historical landslides within the very high susceptibility zone. This study proposes a statistical-physical prior-guided framework for direct five-class landslide susceptibility mapping along the Ancient Qin-Shu Roads in the Qinling-Daba Mountains. A landslide inventory containing 1,407 records and 14 conditioning factors was compiled. First, certainty factor (CF) analysis was used to generate a initial susceptibility map. The Shallow Landsliding Stability model (SHALSTAB) was then introduced to provide a physically meaningful stability mask with which the zonation was corrected and samples of very high, high, moderate, low, and very low susceptibility were constructed. Logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forest (RF), Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer), and Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) were compared under binary and multi-class settings. The results show that RF performed well in both tasks, attaining an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 91.08 % for binary classification and 92.53 % for multi-class classification. In the binary result, the landslide-prone zone occupied 19.3 % of the study area and contained 87.3 % of the historical landslides, yielding a Hit Optimization Index (HOI) of 1.68. In the corresponding multi-class result, the very high susceptibility zone occupied only 13.5 % of the study area while containing 91.8 % of the historical landslides, with an HOI of 1.78. These findings indicate that multi-class learning provides greater historical-landslide coverage and spatial concentration. Compar

papers.title: Elizabeth Williams: Forest Succession on Rainfall-Driven Landslides in the Hauraki Gulf Region, New Zealand
papers.summary: Understanding the ecological consequences of landslide disturbances is increasingly important given the predicted increase in landslide frequency and magnitude under climate change. Steep landforms in the Hauraki Gulf region are prone to shallow landslides driven by high-rainfall storm events. However, there is very limited understanding of the effects of landslide disturbance on vegetation structure and composition in this region. We sampled 18 landslides, spanning 3 to 40+ years post-disturbance, to investigate the roles of age and environmental context in determining successional trajectories. Landslides supported a wide range of predominantly pioneer species. Community composition varied strongly between and within landslides, with patterns associated with site age, geographic position, and soil properties. The prevalence of exotic species classified as problematic weeds increased with proximity to settlements and roads. While increasing landslide activity may enhance landscape-scale heterogeneity, benefiting some ruderal native species, it may also increase opportunities for invasion by exotic species.

papers.title: Slope Stability Focused Condition Assessment, Zion National Park (ZION)
papers.summary: This project was designed to help park managers better understand the susceptibility of select slopes in the park to failure (e.g., rockfall, landslide), and inform management decisions on priority mitigation needs to minimize risk to park staff, visitors, and park assets. The project will assess the condition of select slopes in the park and the probability to failure through evaluating the unique blend of park geologic strata, geologic structure, soils, erosion, slope drainage, and slope failure history. The project work is in parntership with the Federal Highway Administation. The Federal Highway Administration’s Western Federal Lands Highway Division, with support from the National Park Service, U.S. Forest Service, and Bureau of Land Management, has developed a process and guidance (Unstable Slope Management Program (USMP) rating protocol) for assessing slopes at risk to failure through natural processes. papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4888
papers.summary: Abstract. Regional landslide debris inundation hazard assessments commonly rely on scenario-based formulations that require explicit enumeration of discrete landslide events. While effective for local studies, these approaches are computationally intensive, sensitive to scenario design choices, and difficult to apply consistently at regional scales where landslide catalogues are incomplete and long-term behaviour is poorly constrained. In parallel, geomorphological models provide insight into landslide-driven sediment production over long timescales, but are rarely formulated to generate spatially explicit hazard metrics relevant to runout and inundation. Here we present the Landslide Source-to-Inundation Process Model (LS-IPM), a reduced-complexity, process-based framework that reframes landslide debris inundation hazard as a flux-based intensity problem. Rather than simulating discrete landslide scenarios, LS-IPM couples spatially distributed landslide sediment production to mass-conservative, topography-controlled debris routing, producing continuous fields of landslide-derived debris flux. Landslide magnitude and frequency are implicitly linked through a constraint on sediment production, allowing hazard to be evaluated everywhere in the landscape without explicit specification of individual failure events. We apply the LS-IPM to the ~25,000 km² West Coast region of New Zealand at 25 m resolution, generating hazard estimates for present-day conditions, future climate scenarios (RCP6, 2081–2100), and a scenario Alpine Fault Mw 8.0 earthquake. Results show highest debris flux on steep slopes, at the base of high-relief landforms, and along convergent topography, consistent with geomorphological expectations. Approximately 80 % of the region is affected by some degree of landslide debris inundation hazard, with future climate conditions expected to increase mean annual debris flux by ~50 %. papers.title: Disability-inclusive disaster management in India integrating healthcare, the National Building Code and Indian Public Health Standards: a narrative review
papers.source: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health
papers.summary: India’s disaster management framework, established under the Disaster Management Act of 2005, addresses hazards like floods, cyclones, earthquakes, heatwaves, landslides, and heavy rain. However, the 26.8 million people with disabilities in India 2.21% of the population per the 2011 Census, with global estimates suggesting up to 15-24.9% face disproportionate risks, including mortality rates up to four times higher than others. Despite increased healthcare spending (from 1.2% of GDP in 2014-15 to 2.1% in 2022-23) and programs like Ayushman Bharat and Niramaya Health Insurance, many healthcare facilities and disaster shelters remain inaccessible for persons with disabilities. The National Building Code (NBC) of 2016 and Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) of 2022 set standards for accessible infrastructure and emergency preparedness, yet compliance is inconsistent. This narrative review explores how integrating healthcare, building codes, and public health standards can foster a disability-inclusive disaster management system. It highlights barriers, such as inaccessible shelters, limited disaster management training for persons with disabilities, and attitudinal challenges, and suggests solutions like retrofitting facilities, developing Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) materials/Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), and boosting community involvement to ensure equitable safety.

Uso de modelos multinivel para incorporar la heterogeneidad espacial en la evaluación de la susceptibilidad de movimientos en masa
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility is defined as the likelihood of landslide occurrence under favorable terrain conditions. Traditional logistic regression models often fall short by assuming spatial homogeneity, ignoring the inherent variability of physical and environmental factors. To overcome this limitation, multilevel models that incorporate both fixed and random effects to capture variability among different spatial units are used. In this study, a multilevel logistic regression model is employed to assess landslide susceptibility in the Colombian Andes, incorporating both natural hydrological divisions and clustering-based spatial techniques. This approach provides a more nuanced representation of susceptibility by addressing geographic heterogeneity. Two regionalization approaches are tested: natural basin divisions (Atrato, Cauca, Magdalena), and spatial clustering derived from morphometric characteristics. The results reveal that basin-based regionalization achieves a better model fit based on Akaike (AIC) and Bayesian (BIC) information criteria metrics compared to the spatio-clustering model. This suggests that hydrological boundaries are more consistent in capturing landslide dynamics in the study area, likely due to their alignment with geomorphological processes. The fixed and random effect coefficients illustrate that variables such as elevation, relief, and area have significant variability depending on the regionalization method used. A major advantage of using multilevel models is their ability to incorporate spatial variability without artificially dividing the study area and training separate models for each subregion. By using shared information between different spatial units, these models can improve the estimation of both global and local landslide effects.

papers.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23063155. A comprehensive reading of this preprint reveals a major technical discrepancy that must be resolved before a full scientific evaluation can take place. There appears to be an unintended mix-up between two completely different manuscripts during the submission process. The main title specifically focuses on topographic factors and human-land relationships within land-use patterns. However, the abstract provided right below it details an entirely separate study on three-dimensional (3D) transient electromagnetic (TEM) imaging, landslide fracture zones, and hydraulic fracturing parameters. Land-use planning dynamics and geophysical resistivity observations represent completely distinct fields of research. This mismatch extends to the keywords and the official subject classification of "Geophysics and Geology," which do not align with the focus promised in the title. It is highly likely that an incorrect abstract text block or document version was uploaded to the server. The authors should address this structural layout error immediately, withdraw the current version, and upload the correct matching manuscript text to allow for a proper peer review. papers.title: Defense Management in Disaster Management in Depok City: Strengthening Inter-agency Synergy to Support National Resilience
papers.summary: This article examines defense management in disaster management in Depok City with an emphasis on strengthening inter-agency synergy to support national resilience. The study uses a qualitative descriptive approach based on document analysis and secondary data, including Indonesian disaster-management regulations, national policy documents, official information published by the Depok City Government, and relevant disaster-management literature. The analysis focuses on institutional roles, coordination, preparedness, operational response, resource mobilization, information exchange, and the contribution of civil-military cooperation to local resilience. The study finds that disaster management in Depok requires an integrated approach because flood, landslide, storm, fire, and other urban hazards can affect public services, mobility, infrastructure, and community security simultaneously. Official Depok Government information demonstrates the importance of joint preparedness involving local government, TNI-Polri, firefighters and rescue personnel, PMI, and disaster volunteers. The analysis further identifies four strategic requirements: an integrated command and coordination mechanism, interoperable information and communication, joint preparedness and resource planning, and continuous evaluation through exercises and after-action review. From a defense-management perspective, TNI support should be understood within the legal framework for disaster assistance and as part of a broader national resilience system rather than as a substitute for civilian disaster-management institutions. The article proposes an inter-agency disaster resilience framework for Depok that connects risk information, preparedness, response, recovery, and institutional learning. The framework is intended to strengthen the capacity of local government and stakeholders to maintain essential services and protect the population during complex disasters

papers.title: Denali Park Road geophysical investigation
papers.summary: The Denali Park Road Geophysical Investigation, led by the US Army Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) in partnership with the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), evaluated permafrost extent and geotechnical risks along critical segments of Denali National Park and Preserve’s road corridor. Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) and electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) were used to assess subsurface conditions and identify areas vulnerable to permafrost degradation, differential settlement, and related hazards threatening infrastructure stability. Surveys were conducted at five key locations: the park entrance, Riley Creek Campground, Kennel Bus Loop, Savage River, and Bear Cave Landslide. These methods detected permafrost layers, sediment structures, saturated soils, and hydrological anomalies. Data collected in August 2024 guided targeted borehole drilling to confirm and refine geophysical interpretations. Preliminary results revealed ice-rich permafrost, saturated zones, and clay horizons associated with ground instability and landslide potential. GPR identified strong dielectric contrasts suggestive of subsurface water, while ERT pinpointed low-resistivity zones likely indicating thaw-sensitive soils. The integration of geophysical and borehole data provided critical insights into subsurface conditions, supporting future engineering decisions for maintaining the safety and resilience of Denali Park Road.

Integrated remote sensing and geotechnical investigations of the 2022 Jiujiawan mudstone landslide in Xining city, China: from deformation monitoring to failure mechanisms
papers.source: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
papers.summary: Mudstone landslides are widespread worldwide, with their initiation and evolution mainly governed by the coupled effects of rock mass microstructure and hydromechanical behavior. However, the linkage between Earth observation (EO)-derived deformation signals and microscale weakening mechanisms remains poorly constrained. Using the catastrophic Jiujiawan landslide (15 September 2022, Xining, China) as a case study, this research aims to reconstruct the spatiotemporal evolution of the landslide and explain the multiscale mechanisms connecting microscale material degradation with macroscale slope failure through evidence-based interpretation. To achieve this, an integrated framework combining multisource EO data, geotechnical investigations, and laboratory analyses was applied. This approach clarifies deformation characteristics and failure mechanisms from coupled macro- and microscale perspectives. At the macroscopic scale, a high-fidelity three-dimensional model was reconstructed using unmanned aerial vehicle photogrammetry. Satellite optical imagery was used to qualitatively trace the pre-failure evolutionary trajectory, complemented by interferometric synthetic aperture radar to quantitatively reconstruct spatiotemporal displacement sequences. At the microscopic scale, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive spectroscopy characterized the mineralogical suite and microstructural fabric. These analyses reveal the properties of Paleogene mudstone intercalated with gypsum layers, showing how pore-fracture networks accelerate rock mass degradation. Synthesis of the results indicates a process-based linkage whereby microscale hydromechanical weakening (clay mineral hydration, argillization, and gypsum dissolution) is progressively manifested as macroscopic creep and acceleration in EO-derived displacement time series, with seismic preconditioning (the 2022 Ms 6.9 Menyuan earthquake) further reducing the slope’s structural threshold through

papers.title: Multi-Scale Landslide Displacement Prediction and Multi-Level Early Warning for the Three Gorges Reservoir Area Using Multi-Source Sensing and Gated-Attention Multimodal Fusion
papers.summary: Landslides are severe global geological hazards, and landslide displacement prediction is essential for early warning. Focusing on landslides induced by the coupling of periodic reservoir water level fluctuations and local short-term rainstorms in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area (TGRA), existing early-warning methods suffer from coarse rainfall spatial representation, static multimodal-feature fusion, and insufficient deformation-stage-based hierarchical warning mechanisms. Based on multi-source sensing data including Global Positioning System (GPS) displacement monitoring, reservoir water level sensors, ground rain gauges, meteorological radar, and multi-timescale rainfall forecast maps, this study integrates multimodal time-series records of multiple landslide sites from 2007 to 2024. Particle Swarm Optimization–Kriging (PSO–Kriging) interpolation and rainfall-map gridding were employed to construct a dual-source fine-grained rainfall reconstruction scheme. The Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM)–Attention network extracted deep temporal features, and a gated-attention fusion mechanism realized 1 d–15 d multi-scale landslide displacement prediction. Combined with the five-stage landslide creep theory, a four-level early-warning system was established. Experimental results show that the proposed multimodal-fusion model achieves a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 3.42 ± 1.27 mm for the 1 d prediction horizon. The model F1-score reaches 89.3 ± 1.9% for short-term warning and 81.7 ± 1.2% for medium-and-long-term warning, which fits well with long-term reservoir-monitoring scenarios. This framework provides feasible technical support for reservoir landslide hazard prevention using multi-source sensing.

papers.title: Reply on RC2
papers.summary: Abstract. Regional landslide susceptibility mapping generally treats landslide/non-landslide discrimination as a binary learning task and subsequently divides predicted probabilities into several qualitative classes. This two-stage strategy does not directly represent the susceptibility gradient and may therefore reduce the spatial concentration of historical landslides within the very high susceptibility zone. This study proposes a statistical-physical prior-guided framework for direct five-class landslide susceptibility mapping along the Ancient Qin-Shu Roads in the Qinling-Daba Mountains. A landslide inventory containing 1,407 records and 14 conditioning factors was compiled. First, certainty factor (CF) analysis was used to generate a initial susceptibility map. The Shallow Landsliding Stability model (SHALSTAB) was then introduced to provide a physically meaningful stability mask with which the zonation was corrected and samples of very high, high, moderate, low, and very low susceptibility were constructed. Logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forest (RF), Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer), and Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) were compared under binary and multi-class settings. The results show that RF performed well in both tasks, attaining an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 91.08 % for binary classification and 92.53 % for multi-class classification. In the binary result, the landslide-prone zone occupied 19.3 % of the study area and contained 87.3 % of the historical landslides, yielding a Hit Optimization Index (HOI) of 1.68. In the corresponding multi-class result, the very high susceptibility zone occupied only 13.5 % of the study area while containing 91.8 % of the historical landslides, with an HOI of 1.78. These findings indicate that multi-class learning provides greater historical-landslide coverage and spatial concentration. Compar

papers.title: Ensemble Learning-Based Impact-Load Severity Appraisal for Offshore Wind Cables Exposed to Submarine Landslide Flows
papers.source: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
papers.summary: Offshore wind power cables may experience drag and lift loading where submarine landslides or related density flows cross a cable corridor. To prioritise conditions for detailed analysis, a leakage-controlled ensemble-learning workflow was developed from multi-source submarine landslide–pipeline/cable impact data and evaluated by source-grouped cross-validation. Separately predicted peak drag and peak lift were converted to empirical percentile ranks and averaged to form a dataset-relative peak-load severity index. The resulting Low–Extreme categories achieved accuracy of 0.748, macro F1 of 0.690 and High/Extreme recall of 0.758; binary High/Extreme identification achieved accuracy of 0.903, F1 of 0.800 and ROC-AUC of 0.947. Missingness analyses gave four-category accuracy of 0.717–0.771 across full, low-missingness and complete-case settings, whereas weight and threshold changes showed that category boundaries remain calibration choices rather than universal limits. Scenario and feature-group results indicate combined associations with hydrodynamic forcing, cable geometry, rheology and exposure/cover conditions. The output is intended to rank candidate conditions for computational fluid dynamics, physical modelling or structural verification. It is not a design load, a code check or a full risk estimate, which would additionally require occurrence probability, cable vulnerability, consequence and project-specific validation.

papers.title: VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT OF HOUSEHOLDS TO NATURAL HAZARDS: A CASE STUDY OF AN ETHNIC COMMUNITY IN LAO CAI PROVINCE, VIETNAM
papers.source: Tạp chí Khoa học Biến đổi khí hậu
papers.summary: This study presents an indicator-based assessment of household vulnerability to natural hazards among H’Mong communities in Lao Cai Province, Vietnam. The assessment used the IPCC AR4 framework with three components: Exposure (E), Sensitivity (S), and Adaptive Capacity (AC), and a set of 19 indicators was used to assess the vulnerability. Household data were collected through in-depth and semi–structured interviews with 70 H’Mong households in 2025. Flash floods and landslides are the most frequently experienced hazards in the study area, with percentages of 67% and 80%, respectively. 100% of interviewed households rely on agriculture. Approximately 73% of households reported having no savings or access to credit, 68.5% lived in wooden, grade IV, or temporary houses, and only 19% had implemented housing reinforcement measures. The calculated assessment results for E, S, and AC were 0.46, 0.57, and 0.44, respectively, resulting in an overall vulnerability index of 0.60. Financial limitations, inadequate housing, and weak institutional support were identified as the main constraints to household resilience. These findings provide evidence to support targeted disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation policies for ethnic minority communities in mountainous regions

papers.title: Reproducibility-Aware Semivariogram Analysis for Geodetic Deformation Monitoring: Two Case Studies from Poland
papers.summary: Mass earth movements require reliable monitoring as well as defensible interpretation of spatial variability. This study evaluates a reproducibility-aware semivariogram workflow using two geodetic datasets with markedly different provenance: a reproducible two-epoch total-station network at the Kadzielnia landslide and archival UAV/Surfer products from a mining-affected road embankment in Bytom. The central question is not whether the two deformation mechanisms can be directly compared, but how much spatial inference remains defensible when sampling support, reference control, and data provenance differ. For Kadzielnia, 27 rock bolts generated 351 unique point pairs. Empirical semivariograms were recalculated with bootstrap confidence intervals, competing nugget, spherical, exponential, and Gaussian models, lag-bin sensitivity tests, leave-one-out kriging, simple prediction baselines, directional semivariograms, and circular statistics. Under the primary binning scheme, dh is best represented by a pure nugget, whereas dX, dY, and dr show non-unique model fits and parameter sensitivity; prediction gains over simple baselines are small. Horizontal directions are strongly concentrated (R = 0.970), but the archived network adjustment does not permit exclusion of common-mode reference-frame translation or orientation bias. For Bytom, recovered 2018 and 2019 point clouds contain more than 25 million records per epoch, but a coarse translation-only diagnostic leaves a 0.627 m centered residual RMSE, much larger than the deformation scale of interest. In addition, the exact time interval and point-level provenance of the archived semivariograms cannot be reconstructed. Consequently, Bytom is used only as an archival reproducibility example. The results show that semivariograms are useful exploratory diagnostics, but physical interpretation requires stable reference control, stationarity checks, robust binning, transparent model comparison, and reproducible data provenance.

papers.title: EPISODES OF SLOPE FAILURE ON THE NORTHERN EMPEROR SEAMOUNTS СHAIN AND THE SUBMARINE LANDSLIDES FORMATION
papers.source: Bulletin of Kamchatka Regional Association «Educational-Scientific Center» Earth Sciences
papers.summary: Slope failures and submarine landslides formation in the northern Emperor Seamounts Chain, the northern section of the Hawaiian-Emperor Ridge, were studied using bathymetric and seismic data. These data were obtained during cruise SO201-1a on the research vessel Sonne, carried out in frames of the Russian- German KALMAR project. Their analysis made it possible to identify submarine landslides and mass transport deposits, which were formed as a result of four episodes of slope failure. The two episodes could be caused by active growth of volcanoes, during which their edifices are unstable and seismic activity is the highest. The first occurred when edifices were forming over the Hawaiian hotspot. The second episode is likely related to the reactivation of volcanism that occurred due to the change of the Kula Plate motion in Eocene. The slope failure during the third and fourth episodes was likely caused by the formation of unstable sediment volumes. This material was carried out of the Bering Sea, forming the Meiji Drift, and its volume increased as the Emperor Seamounts Chain approached the Aleutian Island arc.
